name: PT Uni-Charm Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Uni-Charm Indonesia: a net-cash converter priced for a permanent loss
frontmatter.summary: UCID fell to a headline loss in FY2025 on a fixed-asset impairment and a prior-year tax charge, not on a collapse in cash generation, and its 2026 profit is mostly non-operating. At Rp388 the market pays 0.3x of book for a business holding 1,803 IDR bn of cash. We initiate BUY with a Rp704 target, a 81.7% total return, on cash conversion and the balance sheet, not on a profit re-rating.
thesis: The FY2025 loss is not the run-rate. 301 IDR bn of it is a fixed-asset impairment and 286 IDR bn a prior-year tax charge, both struck below the operating line; the operating loss itself is -522.6 after 489.0 of depreciation and a 197 IDR bn trade-receivable write-down, and on EBITDA the year was essentially breakeven at -33.6 [S6].
The balance sheet is the floor. Cash of 1,803 IDR bn against debt that is entirely the lease liability of 970 IDR bn leaves the shares at 0.3x of book [S2].

Revenue is growing again but the profit is not operating. Nine-month revenue reached 6,622 IDR bn, ahead of the prior year, while selling and administrative costs consumed all but a sliver of the gross profit [S2].
The margin, not the top line, is the bet. We hold the gross margin at 22.5% and take the operating margin to 2.7% by FY2030E [S0].
At these thin margins growth destroys value, so the price is not paying for a re-rating. The DCF earns its return from cash conversion and the balance sheet, not from a higher multiple [S2].

catalysts.event: Q4 2026 trading and the exit gross margin, the number that decides whether the FY2026 recovery holds
FY2026 audited results and the proposed final dividend under the stated payout policy
Annual general meeting: dividend approval and any update on the parent royalty and related-party terms

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Uni-Charm Indonesia with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp704 against a last price of Rp388: 81.5% of price upside and 81.7% of total return with the dividend counted. The target is the probability-weighted blend of our three DCF cases, rolled twelve months forward at the cost of equity and cut by the 10.0% liquidity discount the engine applies to a register with a 20.0% free float. The DCF is the only method we weight, because the earnings cross-check is corrupted by a deferred-tax credit and the market multiple is distorted by a trough EBITDA. The build is: base-case value Rp734 a share rolled forward at the cost of equity, blended with the bear and bull cases in the ratio fifty-five, thirty, fifteen, then cut by the 10.0% liquidity discount to the Rp704 target - the bear case is Rp104 as a present value and Rp119 twelve months out in the scenario table. The target sits below the base case because the third quarter gave back the first half's operating profit and the bear therefore carries a larger weight than the bull. The recommendation is not a call that the shares re-rate to their old multiple; it is a cash-flow claim. A business that still converts its depreciation into cash is being valued by the market as if the FY2025 loss were permanent.

What the market is pricing is the loss, and we think it is pricing it wrong. FY2025 net profit was -1,195.1, a swing of more than a trillion rupiah from FY2024, and a reader who stops at the headline will assume the franchise broke [S6]. It did not break; it was written down. The year contains 301 IDR bn of fixed-asset impairment and a 286 IDR bn prior-year tax charge, both struck below the operating line, and its EBIT of -522.6 on 7,984.4 of revenue is arrived at after 489.0 of depreciation and a 197 IDR bn trade-receivable write-down inside administrative costs. On EBITDA the year was essentially breakeven at -33.6, and operating cash flow stayed positive and was higher than in FY2024 [S6]. The market has capitalised the accounting event, not the economics.

The business we are buying is the Indonesian arm of Unicharm Corporation, which holds 59.2% of the shares and supplies the technology, the brands and the royalty agreement, with the Sinar Mas pulp and paper arm PT APP Purinusa Ekapersada holding a further 20.8% [S6]. It makes and sells baby diapers under MamyPoko, feminine care under Charm and CharmNap, adult care under Lifree and pet care under Deli Joy, in two reportable segments that the company calls diapers and non-diapers [S2]. Diapers are the bigger half by revenue and the weaker half by profit: in the first nine months of 2026 they produced 4,824 IDR bn of revenue and 1,066 IDR bn of gross profit, while non-diapers produced 1,799 IDR bn and 497 IDR bn [S2]. The mix matters because the higher-margin feminine and adult categories are where management says the improvement is coming from, and where the nine-month numbers show it already arriving [S7].

The balance sheet is unusually strong for a company this small. At 30 September 2026 UCID held 1,803 IDR bn of cash against 970 IDR bn of lease liabilities - all of its debt is lease, with no bank borrowing drawn - so net cash is a large share of the market capitalisation and the operating business a small fraction of it [S2]. Book equity was 4,623.4 and the shares trade at 0.3x of book [S0]. The cash is already credited at face value in our DCF bridge: every rupiah of it sits in the Rp734 value and therefore in the Rp704 target. That is why we do not model a special dividend as a value event. Distributing the cash would not create value in this arithmetic - it would move cash from the company's balance sheet to the holder's, leaving intrinsic value per share unchanged - so the case does not need a distribution scenario; it needs the market to stop pricing the cash at a discount. The stated policy is a fifth of net profit and the board paid it through the FY2025 loss, which is observed rather than assumed [S6], and nothing after the balance-sheet date points to a special distribution [S4]. The cash is real, and it is the reason the downside is bounded.

Three things move the value, in order. The gross margin path is worth more than everything else, because at these thin operating margins a single point of gross margin is a large share of EBIT; we hold the margin at 22.5% through 22.5%, a point below the nine-month actual, above the FY2025 like-for-like and below the FY2024 like-for-like once freight is put back on the same basis [S2]. Capex is second: nine-month cash capex was 26.9 IDR bn, a fraction of depreciation, and the moment that under-investment ends the free cash flow falls [S2]. Net cash is third, and it is the reason we can underwrite the downside. The tax shield is a fourth, minor item: the forecast uses a reduced effective rate for three years against the unrecognised losses and deferred tax assets, worth a few rupiah a share rather than the material uplift a full shield would imply, because the profit base it shelters is small [S6]. At 11.1x of our FY2027E earnings the shares are not statistically cheap on the profit line, which is why the case rests on the balance sheet and on margin normalisation rather than on a low multiple [S0].

The case against us is real and it is the third quarter, and the reported profit is not operating. The first half earned 116 IDR bn of operating profit; the nine months then closed with the gross profit of 1,563 IDR bn almost entirely consumed by selling expenses of 1,357 IDR bn and administrative costs of 195 IDR bn, so the third quarter gave the first half back [S2][S3]. The nine-month net profit of 61.5 IDR bn is not evidence of an operating recovery: pre-tax profit of 36.9 IDR bn was built from finance income of 40.0 IDR bn, other income of 23.8 IDR bn and a tax credit of 24.5 IDR bn on a very small operating base, and operating cash flow was -9.2 IDR bn [S2]. If imported pulp and superabsorbent polymer costs stay where the rupiah and the input cycle have put them, the base case is too high and the bear case of Rp104 a share, Rp119 twelve months out, is the right one [S0]. The stock is also barely traded, so a position of any size cannot be built or exited quickly, which is why the engine applies a liquidity discount and why we size this as a value claim rather than a trading one [S0].

PT Uni-Charm Indonesia manufactures and sells disposable hygiene products in Indonesia and exports a small share of output. The company reports two operating segments, diapers and non-diapers, both located in Indonesia, and describes its line of business as sanitary napkins, night wings, panty liners, baby diapers and pet care [S2]. The brand portfolio runs from MamyPoko in baby care through Charm and CharmNap in feminine care to Lifree in adult care, Deli Joy in pet care and Kirei in wipes [S0]. The company was founded in 1997, listed in 2019 and is headquartered in South Jakarta, with factories in the KIIC industrial estate at Karawang in West Java and the Ngoro industrial park at Mojokerto in East Java [S6].

The segment split is the first thing to understand about the profit and loss. In the nine months to 30 September 2026 diapers produced 4,824 IDR bn of the group's 6,622 IDR bn net revenue, or about three-quarters, and non-diapers 1,799 IDR bn [S2]. Gross profit told a different story: diapers earned 1,066 IDR bn and non-diapers 497 IDR bn, so the smaller segment earned just under a third of the gross profit at a visibly higher margin [S2]. After selling and administrative costs the diaper segment was loss-making and the non-diaper segment carried the group, which is the structural fact behind the FY2025 loss and the FY2026 recovery [S2]. Management's own explanation of the recovery is exactly this mix shift: a higher contribution from feminine care lifted the gross margin ratio, supported by general trade, e-commerce and receivables management [S7].

The product strategy is a tiered one. MamyPoko is sold at premium, mid-range and affordable price points, in tape and pants formats, with the premium end carrying the innovation story and the affordable end defending volume against local brands [S6]. Charm covers sanitary napkins and panty liners, including a bio-material and organic-cotton line launched in 2025, and Lifree addresses adult incontinence, a category that grows with the population's age structure rather than its birth rate [S6]. Pet care under Deli Joy is small but growing and was showcased at the Indonesia International Pet Expo in 2025 [S6]. The company also sells non-woven material through a subsidiary and earns research income from its parent [S2].

The competitive position is leader in baby and feminine care and challenger in adult care by the company's own account, and the board's 2025 report is candid that new lower-priced entrants and consumer down-trading eroded share in both diapers and sanitary pads during the year [S6]. Unicharm's own history records MamyPoko reaching the number one market-share position in Indonesia in 2003, which is the origin of the franchise but also a reminder of how old the leadership is [S6]. The edge is technology and brand: the parent licenses the trademarks and manufacturing know-how, and the local company pays a royalty of a low single-digit percentage of net sales for the privilege [S2]. That licence is an advantage in product quality and a permanent cost that a local challenger does not carry.

Distribution is the operational lever management is pulling. The company sells through modern trade, general trade and e-commerce, and the 2026 commentary emphasises strengthening the general-trade network, widening product exposure and pushing online sales [S7]. That is the right response to down-trading, because the consumer who trades down does so in neighbourhood shops rather than in hypermarkets, but it is expensive: selling expenses were 1,357 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026, up sharply on the prior year, and part of that increase is the freight reclassification discussed in the financials [S2]. The trade-off between defending shelf space and protecting margin is the central operating tension in the name.

The group structure is simple and the controlling shareholder is the reason. The register has three blocks, per the annual report's share-ownership table: Unicharm Corporation of Japan holds 59.2%, PT APP Purinusa Ekapersada - the pulp and paper arm of the Sinar Mas group - holds 20.8%, and the public holds 20.0% [S6]. There is no intermediate listed holding company and no family conglomerate above Unicharm, but the second block is a strategic Indonesian conglomerate with board representation: the APP bloc appears among the related parties in the notes and its nominees sit on the board [S6]. The governance question is therefore two-sided: transfer pricing and the royalty to the Japanese parent, and the commercial relationship - including raw-material supply - with the Sinar Mas side. Either can move value without the minority's consent [S2][S6]. The company employed 2,003 people at the last count, small for a manufacturer with two industrial estates, because the plants are capital-intensive [S0].

Strategy for 2026 and beyond, as stated in the annual report, is to grow the value-added categories, re-arrange the product portfolio toward higher-margin items, improve efficiency and optimise working capital, with the explicit expectation of better profitability in 2026 [S6]. The company also continues to invest behind the brands through television and digital campaigns, distributor partnerships, midwife and health-post education programmes and the feminine-care and adult-care launches, and reports the pet-care and wipes extensions as part of the same push [S6]. There is no stated plan to sell assets, restructure the balance sheet or change the dividend policy.

Indonesia's disposable-hygiene market is a volume business with a long runway and a shrinking baby cohort. Per-capita diaper use is low by regional standards and modern-trade penetration is uneven across the archipelago, which supports category growth; against that, the birth rate has been falling for a decade, which caps the baby-diaper pool and pushes growth toward feminine, adult and pet care. The category is price-segmented, and the fastest-growing part in a weak-consumption year is the affordable end, where local converters compete on cost rather than brand. That is the structural backdrop against which a premium multinational brand has to defend share.

The Indonesian personal and household products category that UCID competes in is best understood as three adjacent markets with three different demand drivers: baby diapers, feminine hygiene and adult incontinence, plus a small pet-care and wipes business. All three are branded, all three reach the consumer through the same general-trade and modern-trade channels, and all three share a cost base of absorbent pulp, non-woven fabric and superabsorbent polymer [S2]. That shared cost base is why the segments move together at the gross-margin line even when their demand drivers do not, and it is why the input-cost cycle dominates near-term earnings for the whole group. The company does not disclose market-size data in its annual report, so this report puts no market-size number on the category.

Demand in FY2025 was weak, and the company says why. The board's report describes intense competition in the diaper and sanitary-pad segments driven by new entrants at lower price points, against sluggish purchasing power, which pushed consumers toward cheaper products in a classic down-trading pattern and pressured the company's share [S6]. The management discussion repeats the diagnosis and adds that the economy grew solidly while household consumption did not keep pace [S6]. That is a demand-mix shock rather than a demand-level shock: the category did not disappear, the willingness to pay a premium for a multinational brand fell. For a company whose gross margin depends on a premium price, that is the most damaging kind of competition.

The input side is import-dependent and dollar-denominated, and the house has a source for it. Indonesia has one domestic superabsorbent-polymer producer with capacity of 90,000 t against domestic demand of about 100,000 t, and the producer plans to expand while imports still arrive because foreign petrochemical capacity is in oversupply [S8]. The same source records that pulp and other petrochemical inputs are imported and that the rupiah is the transmission channel [S8]. This matters twice: it explains why UCID's gross margin is a spread over a dollar cost base rather than a local manufacturing margin, and it explains why the third-quarter margin broke when the currency and freight costs moved against the company [S2]. The house macro deck carries a usd_idr path but no pulp or superabsorbent-polymer price series, and the industry template's only cost link is the agri deck's CPO series, which prices neither input; we therefore cannot wire the currency into cost of revenue as a deck variable and the link is set to zero in the assumptions. The FX channel is modelled instead as a gross-margin shock in the bear case, sized to the rupiah path the macro deck assumes [S0][S8].

The cost pass-through question is the heart of the industry analysis. A branded leader can pass input inflation on if it has pricing power; a leader losing share to cheaper alternatives cannot, because a price increase accelerates the down-trading it is already suffering [S6]. UCID's own results show the asymmetry: in the first nine months of 2026 revenue grew 9.2% while the gross margin recovered only because input costs eased against a weak prior-year base, and in the third quarter the margin fell sharply when costs rose again [S2]. We therefore set the cost link and its pass-through to zero rather than assume the company recovers input inflation through price [S6]. That is not a cautious haircut; it is what the last two years show.

Competition is fragmented at the low end and concentrated at the high end. The premium tier is contested by multinational brands, including the company's own MamyPoko and its principal international rivals, while the affordable tier is contested by local converters who buy imported polymer and pulp on the spot market and compete on pack price [S6]. The company's advantage is technology, brand trust and the parent's product pipeline; its disadvantage is a cost structure that carries a royalty to the parent and a premium brand's marketing budget [S2]. In a down-trading market the disadvantage dominates, which is what happened in FY2025, and the company's response of pushing general trade and e-commerce and leaning on feminine care is an attempt to compete where brand still matters.

Five-forces view. Supplier power is high and rising, because the key inputs are imported and concentrated and the domestic polymer alternative is still short of demand [S8]. Buyer power is high in the affordable tier, where switching costs are close to zero and price is the decision variable [S6]. The threat of new entrants is high at the low end, as the 2025 share loss demonstrates, and low at the premium end, where brand and technology are real barriers [S6]. Substitutes are limited for diapers and feminine care but real in adult care, where institutional products compete. Rivalry is intense and increasing, and the board describes it that way [S6]. On that reading the industry earns a modest return on capital in the long run, which is consistent with UCID's thin operating margin and its low return on equity of 4.6% in our terminal year [S0].

Regulation touches the category in three places: product registration and halal certification for hygiene products, import duties and licensing on the raw materials, and environmental rules on single-use plastics that raise the bar for product design [S6]. The company reports quality, environmental and medical-device certifications and a solar-power installation at two factories as part of its sustainability programme, and it discloses no material regulatory sanction in the year [S6]. For valuation purposes the regulatory risk is a cost risk rather than an existential one: the categories are legal, essential and politically sensitive on price, which caps pricing power. It is not a licence that can be withdrawn, unlike the mining names in this book.

The moat is narrower than the brand suggests. The company has a genuine intangible asset in MamyPoko and Charm, protected by the parent's trademarks, and a distribution footprint built over two decades [S6]. But the FY2025 experience shows that the brand did not protect price when the consumer traded down, and the royalty arrangement means part of the brand's value accrues to the parent rather than to the Indonesian minority [S2]. We therefore do not give the company a no-fade DCF. Our model fades growth to the terminal rate over ten years and assumes the operating margin never returns to the FY2024 level of 4.5%, which is the honest reading of a franchise that has just lost share in its core category [S6].

The first job in the financials is to restate what the data pack gets wrong, and on this name it gets two things wrong. The pack carries FY2025 D&A of a small fraction of the true charge, because Indonesian filings use the direct cash-flow method and the pack's line captures only part of the note [S0]. The notes show fixed-asset depreciation plus right-of-use depreciation of 489 IDR bn in FY2025 and 486 IDR bn in FY2024 [S6].

The second error is the operating result. The pack takes a 197 IDR bn trade-receivable impairment out of FY2025 administrative expenses, against 19.4 IDR bn in FY2024, and folds the 28.3 IDR bn other tax expense into operating costs, so the EBIT it carries appears nowhere in the consolidated profit and loss [S0][S6]. We restate both years by line from that statement: selling and administrative costs of 1,724 IDR bn in FY2025 and 1,540 IDR bn in FY2024, EBIT of -522.6 and 434.9, and EBITDA of -33.6 and 920.9 on the restated depreciation [S6]. Keeping the receivable impairment inside operating costs rather than excluding it as a one-off is deliberate: it is a credit-loss charge the auditor booked against the receivables book, so the operating history is shown as signed and the recovery case has to be argued against that base. The engine now rebuilds both EBITDA and EBIT from those facts, and the forecast is struck on the same presentation, so the FY2025 comparator is on the LK basis rather than the pack's [S6]. Without the D&A restatement every margin and every multiple in this report would be wrong by a factor of several.

The second adjustment is a reclassification rather than an error, and it needs a bridge. Freight sat inside cost of revenue in the prior years: 496 IDR bn in FY2024 and 405 IDR bn in FY2025, against 331 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2025 and only 33.6 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026, because the company moved the line into selling expenses [S2][S6]. The reported history and the 2026 actual are therefore on different bases. Put the freight back into cost of revenue and the FY2024 gross margin is about a quarter and the FY2025 margin about a fifth; a reader who compares the FY2025 reported margin with the reported nine-month 2026 figure without that adjustment will overstate the improvement. Our forecast is set on the current presentation and holds the long-run margin at 22.5%, a point below the nine-month gross profit of 1,563 IDR bn on revenue of 6,622 IDR bn and between the two restated full years; the assumptions file carries the full like-for-like bridge, including the fact that the operating margin is unchanged by the reclassification because freight moved between two lines below it.

Revenue history tells a three-act story. FY2024 revenue was 9,675.5, FY2025 fell -17.5% to 7,984.4 on the diaper volume loss and down-trading, and the first nine months of 2026 recovered to 6,622 IDR bn [S6][S2]. The FY2025 decline was concentrated in the fourth quarter, which is why the FY2026 growth rate in our model looks high at 9.2% even though it merely annualises a normal fourth quarter on top of nine months that grew at a mid-single-digit rate [S2]. We forecast 3.5% growth from FY2027E, which is flat in real terms against the macro deck's inflation and below nominal GDP [S0].

Margins are the whole debate. The reported history reads 18.3% in FY2022, 19.8% in FY2023, 20.4% in FY2024 and 15.0% in FY2025, but only the 2026 figures are struck on the presentation the company now uses; on a like-for-like basis the two full years are higher by the freight line and the nine-month actual is 1,563 IDR bn on 6,622 IDR bn [S0][S2]. Our forecast holds 22.5% for FY2026E and 22.5% by FY2030E: a point below the nine-month average and between the two restated full years. That is a price-and-mix judgement about permanent down-trading, not a cost recovery, and it does not assume the margin gets back to the FY2024 like-for-like level [S0][S6]; the assumptions file carries the bridge. The exit rate is the risk: the third quarter was materially weaker than the first half, which is why the bear case shocks the margin down rather than up. Operating margin follows: 4.5% in FY2024, -6.5% in FY2025 and -0.3% in our FY2026E, reaching 2.7% by FY2030E, all on the restated LK basis [S6]. That is a business earning a thin spread, and the valuation respects it.

The cost base is dominated by materials and by selling spend. Raw materials and semi-finished goods are the largest line in cost of revenue, direct labour and depreciation follow, and selling expenses carry the royalty to the parent, the distribution costs and the advertising [S2]. The related-party royalty was 168 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 and related-party purchases of materials were 1.9% of cost of revenue [S2]. Those are not abuses - they are the price of the parent's technology and supply chain - but they are permanent value leakage to the controlling shareholder that a minority holder cannot renegotiate, and they are why the company's margin is structurally below what a standalone brand would earn [S2].

Cash flow is where the headline misleads in the company's favour. Operating cash flow stayed positive through the loss year and was higher than in FY2024, but the first nine months of 2026 produced -9.2 IDR bn of operating cash flow despite a reported net profit of 61.5 IDR bn [S2][S6]. The profit is not operating. Pre-tax profit of 36.9 IDR bn was assembled from finance income of 40.0 IDR bn, other income of 23.8 IDR bn, a foreign-exchange loss of 9.6 IDR bn, finance costs of 26.5 IDR bn and other tax expense of 2.3 IDR bn, on top of a gross profit of 1,563 IDR bn that selling expenses of 1,357 IDR bn and administrative costs of 195 IDR bn had almost entirely consumed [S2]. The tax line then added a credit of 24.5 IDR bn. Strip the non-operating items and the company earned a small operating profit in nine months, and less than that in cash: working capital absorbed the difference as inventories and tax-refund claims rose [S2]. The accruals screen is not yet at the level that condemns the earnings, but the direction is wrong and cash conversion has deteriorated sharply, which is why we do not capitalise the FY2026 profit at a multiple [S2]. The method card's accrual test is a warning here, not a kill.

Capex has been cut to the bone and that flatters free cash flow. Cash purchases of fixed assets were 26.9 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 and 85.9 in FY2025, against depreciation of 489 IDR bn [S2][S6]. A company spending a fraction of its depreciation is harvesting an asset base, and the FY2025 impairment and asset disposals shrank that base further [S6]. Our forecast lifts capex from 1.0% of revenue in FY2026E to a replacement rate by FY2030E, which is the honest assumption: current free cash flow is partly a liquidation of the asset base, and the terminal value must not capitalise it [S2]. That is why terminal capex equals roughly terminal depreciation in the model.

The balance sheet is strong and its debt is entirely a lease, not a loan. At 30 September 2026 cash was 1,803 IDR bn and total debt was 970 IDR bn of lease liabilities, with no drawn bank facility [S2]. The increase from the prior year-end is one contract: a 890 IDR bn addition of right-of-use assets for a buildings lease owed to a third-party lessor - the note is explicit that the lease is payable to third parties rather than to a related party, and it does not name the counterparty [S2]. The note states no lease term; its maturity table puts 826 IDR bn of the undiscounted payments in 2031 and later, a tail that runs at the annual rate of the 2027 payment for roughly seven further years [S2]. The fixed payments are 122 IDR bn in 2027 and 1,342 IDR bn undiscounted over the whole term, against a cost base that management treats as largely variable [S2]. We treat the liability as debt: the annual lease charge sits in the profit and loss as depreciation and interest, the free cash flow adds that depreciation back and excludes the principal repayment, and the discounted cash flow deducts the full liability from enterprise value [S2]. Treating it the other way - as rent inside operating costs and no liability - would give a similar equity value, but it would hide the operating leverage: a fixed payment of that size cannot be flexed if demand stays weak, which is why the bear case adds a point of opex [S2].

Capital allocation is conservative and parent-directed. The company pays a stated 20.0% of net profit, paid 70.1 to shareholders in FY2025 and 27.7 in 2026 after the loss, and holds the rest as cash [S2][S6]. There is no buyback, no treasury stock and no rights issue in the period covered by the annual report [S6]. The cash pile earns a deposit yield rather than funding growth, which is why our model has the cash balance rising to 3,678.2 by FY2030E and why the net cash position is such a large share of the value [S0]. At the last price the market capitalisation is below the gross cash balance, which is the clearest statement of the mispricing and of the risk that the cash is simply not returned. A minority investor is effectively buying a deposit account with a consumer franchise attached, and the franchise has to earn its keep on the margin line; the policy payout, not a special distribution, is the observable benchmark and it is what we model [S6].

Earnings-quality flags, run through the house method card. The accruals screen comes first: profit less operating cash flow is positive and worsening in FY2026, and the profit is boosted by a deferred-tax credit rather than by cash [S2]. The divergence screens are neutral: receivables have not outgrown revenue, and the inventory build is explained by working capital rather than by channel stuffing [S2]. The IDX regime screen is clean, with no special monitoring board and no special notation in the material we hold [S6]. Related-party gravity is material but disclosed and priced, with the royalty at 168 IDR bn and purchases at 1.9% of cost of revenue [S2]. Structure flags are mild: a single controlling shareholder, a small free float, no pledge disclosure and a Big Four auditor [S6]. We class the accounting issues as optics-class, not manipulation-class.

The forecast in one paragraph. Revenue grows to 8,722.9 in FY2026E and 10,009.8 by FY2030E; gross margin settles at 22.5%; operating margin reaches 2.7%; D&A falls from 357.6 to 300.3 as the impaired asset base runs down; capex rises from 87.2 to 300.3; and cash rises to 3,678.2 because the dividend takes only a fifth of earnings [S0]. The effective tax rate is cut for three years against the 139 IDR bn of unrecognised losses and the 95.5 IDR bn of unrecognised deferred tax assets, then reverts to statutory: a partial, sourced shield that is worth a few rupiah a share, not the material uplift a full shield would give, because the profits it shelters are small [S6]. The calibration gate re-prices FY2026E on FY2025A economics and compares EBITDA margins: 3.8% against -0.4%, a step the engine reads as inside its tolerance because FY2025 was the trough year rather than a run-rate level [S0]. The LK explains the trough: a fourth-quarter revenue collapse took the full-year denominator down with the margin, a 197 IDR bn trade-receivable charge sat inside administrative costs, and the 301 IDR bn fixed-asset impairment and 286 IDR bn prior-year tax charge sit below EBITDA altogether, so the year's EBITDA was essentially nil while the net loss was -1,195.1 [S6]. The nine-month 2026 actual is the better comparator: operating profit there had turned marginally positive and the gross margin was several points above the FY2025 like-for-like, which is the direction the forecast assumes [S2].

We value UCID on a ten-year discounted free cash flow to the firm, with the terminal value set by a growth rate below nominal GDP, and we weight that method alone. The reason is that the standard cross-checks cannot be trusted on this name. A price-to-earnings multiple on FY2026E earnings of 3.5 a share would capitalise a profit that is smaller than the deferred-tax credit and larger than the operating cash flow, so it measures an accounting artefact rather than earning power [S2]. An enterprise-value multiple on trailing EBITDA is unusable because the company holds net cash, which makes enterprise value smaller than the operating business and the multiple meaningless or negative [S0]. The price-to-book cross-check is meaningful as a floor - the shares trade at 0.3x of book - but the engine's historical screen of one and a half times book would value the company at several times the market price, which is a re-rating assumption rather than a valuation [S0]. We therefore show the cross-checks in the table, explain why they disagree, and let the cash flow set the target.

The cost of capital is built from the macro deck and sits inside the house band. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the Indonesian default spread 1.6%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5% [S0]. With an unlevered beta of 0.85, above the house consumer-staples default because UCID's earnings are a thin spread over imported inputs and have swung from a large profit to a large loss inside two years, the levered beta is 1.25, the cost of equity is 14.2% and the WACC is 11.6% [S6]. The cost of debt in the WACC is 9.4%, the macro deck's rupiah risk-free rate plus its corporate debt spread, not the lower rate used to project the interest line: the lease carries an implicit rate well below the market corporate rate, so the deck spread is the conservative choice and it is disclosed here rather than left implicit. The cost of equity is above the house IDR band while the WACC is inside it. We keep it above the band deliberately: the band presumes a stabilised earnings stream and this company has none, so a 0.85 unlevered beta and a 20.0% tradable float are the honest inputs; forcing the cost of equity into the band would understate a risk the bear case already prices. The rate that actually discounts the cash flows is the WACC, and that is inside the band [S0][S6]. The gap between the two is the balance sheet: the engine treats the lease liability and net cash as debt and cash respectively, so the equity weight is 62.4% and the after-tax cost of debt pulls the WACC below the cost of equity. Both the cost of equity above the band and the WACC inside it are disclosed in the table [S0].

The cash-flow forecast behind the DCF is deliberately unheroic. Free cash flow is negative in the stub year because working capital and a thin operating margin absorb cash, then turns positive as the working-capital build reverses and capex stays low, and then declines as capex rises toward the replacement rate [S0]. Terminal value is 40.7% of enterprise value, which is low for a ten-year DCF and is a good sign: most of the value comes from cash we can see rather than from a terminal assumption [S0]. The terminal growth rate is 3.5%, below the macro deck's nominal GDP, because a company losing share in its core category should not be assumed to grow with the economy forever [S0]. Reinvestment in the terminal year is capex equal to depreciation plus working capital at 3.5% of the revenue increment, which comes to roughly a fifth of NOPAT; at that reinvestment rate the 3.5% terminal growth implies a marginal return on new capital close to sixteen per cent, above the 11.6% WACC. The return on the existing asset base is in the low single digits, which is why the terminal value is doing little more than returning the capital employed at cost even though growth is not value-destroying at the margin; the sensitivity grid carries the zero-real-growth cell for the reader who thinks growth should earn less than that. We do not assume a multiple exit, and the implied exit multiple is shown in the valuation table for the reader to test [S0].

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative. The DCF gives Rp734 a share; the earnings screen at 111.8x on FY2026E and 11.1x on FY2027E tells the same story of a profit base that is only starting to recover; and the book-value screen at a historical multiple sits far above the market because the market has never paid book for this company since listing [S0]. The DCF sits between them, which is where a cash-flow valuation of a low-return business should sit: above the trough the market is paying and below the accounting value of the assets. The market price of Rp388 is below the DCF value, which is the source of the upside [S0].

The sensitivity is dominated by the gross margin and the discount rate. A one-point change in the long-run gross margin moves the value by more than the whole dividend, and a one-point change in the WACC moves it by more again, because the cash flows are long-dated and thin [S0]. Revenue growth matters less than either, which is counter-intuitive for a consumer name and is the point: at a 2.7% operating margin the value is a margin story, not a growth story [S0]. Capex matters because current free cash flow depends on under-investment, and a return to a normal capex ratio removes a meaningful slice of near-term cash [S2]. The sensitivity table shows the grid, and the red team should test the margin cells first [S0].

What the price implies is the most careful part of this report. Running the DCF backwards at the last price, the model solves to an FY2027E revenue growth rate of 16.7% against our 3.5% base case. That is not a growth signal and we do not read it as one. At an operating margin of 2.7% and working capital near a sixth of revenue, each additional rupiah of revenue brings in very little operating profit but requires new capex and new receivables; incremental returns are below the cost of capital, so value is not monotonic in growth. The solver has found the upper root - the growth rate at which value has already fallen back to the price - and the same price is reachable at our own growth rate with a materially lower margin. The economically meaningful reading is therefore the margin: today's price is consistent with a gross margin at the bear-case level, not the 22.5% we forecast, which is itself a point below the nine-month actual [S2]. The market is not paying for growth at any price; it is pricing this business as if the third quarter were the future. The difference between us and the market is not the growth rate. It is the margin, and on our margin and an SG&A ratio of a fifth of revenue the equity is worth Rp734 a share [S0].

The multiple-survival test. At our target the enterprise value is the DCF enterprise value, and the implied multiple on FY2027E EBITDA is a low single digit on a business with a thin but positive operating margin [S0]. That is not multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume: it is a modest multiple for a low-return converter and it is below the multiple the shares carried before the loss [S0]. Because the terminal value is a growing perpetuity rather than an exit multiple, the implied exit multiple is disclosed in the table and is in the same range, so the terminal value does not smuggle in a re-rating [S0]. If the reader believes the operating margin cannot exceed breakeven, the bear case of Rp104 a share is the right valuation and the shares are worth about a quarter of today's price; that downside is the reason this is a value claim with a defined floor, not a cheap stock [S0].

The distribution of outcomes, and what the rating depends on. The base case is Rp838 twelve months out, the bear Rp119 and the bull Rp1,907; the base carries the majority of the probability mass, the bear more than the bull because the third quarter is the most recent evidence, and the bull the smaller tail [S0]. The rating does not depend on the bull. Remove it entirely, split the probability mass evenly between base and bear, and the blend after the liquidity discount is still above the last price - it would take a bear weight well above half to bring the target back to the market. What the bull does is widen the margin of safety, not create it. On the cash: in the base and the bull the bridge credits the 30 September net cash of 1,803 IDR bn less 970 IDR bn at face value, while in the bear the present value of the operating losses offsets it, which is why the bear falls below the per-share cash. A distribution would change the form of the return, not its size; the value is in the cash being there and the market not paying for it [S0][S2].

The largest risk is that the Q3 2026 margin is the new normal rather than a trough. The first half's 116 IDR bn of operating profit did not survive the third quarter - the nine-month result is a fraction of it - and nine-month operating cash flow went to -9.2 IDR bn [S2][S3]. The reported nine-month net profit of 61.5 IDR bn does not contradict that: it is built from non-operating income and a tax credit, not from the operating line [S2]. If imported pulp, polymer and freight stay at those levels and the rupiah stays where the macro deck puts it, the gross margin does not recover to our 22.5% and the base case is too high [S8]. Likelihood is medium and impact is high, because a one-point gross-margin miss is a large share of EBIT at these margins and the correction would flow straight into the valuation [S0].

The second risk is competitive: down-trading persists and the premium brand keeps losing share. The board attributes the FY2025 loss to lower-priced entrants and consumer down-trading, and nothing in the 2026 results shows that pressure ending, because revenue grew but selling expenses grew faster [S6][S2]. If the company has to keep buying shelf space and general-trade reach to hold volume, the operating margin stays near breakeven and the value falls toward the bear case. Likelihood is medium-high and impact is high, because this is the mechanism that produced the FY2025 loss in the first place [S6].

The third risk is the related-party relationship with the parent. The royalty was 168 IDR bn in the first nine months and related-party purchases were 1.9% of cost of revenue, both set under agreements with Unicharm Corporation that the minority cannot renegotiate [S2]. A change in the royalty rate, the transfer prices or the licence terms would move value directly and would be decided by the controlling shareholder. Likelihood is low in any single year and impact is medium, and the exposure is disclosed rather than hidden [S2].

The fourth risk is the lease. The group signed a long-dated building lease in 2026 - the note gives no term, but its maturity table carries 826 IDR bn of the payments in 2031 and later - with 122 IDR bn of fixed payments due in 2027 and 1,342 IDR bn undiscounted in total, owed to a third-party lessor the filings do not name [S2]. The liability is on the balance sheet and in our debt line, and the lease charge is in depreciation and interest, so the base case is not ignoring it. The risk is operating leverage: if revenue falls, the payment does not, and the cost structure the model treats as a ratio of sales is partly fixed. That is why the bear case adds a point of opex on top of the margin shock. Likelihood is medium and impact is medium-high, because the lease is small against revenue but large against the operating profit the recovery depends on [S2].

The fifth risk is liquidity and register structure. The free float is 20.0%, Unicharm Corporation holds 59.2% and PT APP Purinusa Ekapersada a further 20.8%, and the three-month average daily traded value is well under a billion rupiah [S6][S0]. A fund cannot build or exit a meaningful position without moving the price, and the shares can trade below fundamental value for years for that reason alone. Likelihood is certain and impact is medium: it does not change the value, but it changes the realised return, which is why the engine applies a liquidity discount and why we do not present the target as an arbitrage [S0].

The sixth risk is currency. UCID earns rupiah and buys imported inputs in dollars, so a weaker rupiah compresses the gross margin with a lag [S8]. The macro deck does not assume a stronger rupiah for FY2027E than spot, and the third-quarter margin break coincided with currency and freight pressure [S0][S2]. The model cannot wire the currency into cost of revenue because no house deck prices pulp or superabsorbent polymer, so the exposure is carried in the bear case's margin shock rather than in a separate FX line; that is a modelling limitation and it is stated rather than hidden [S0]. Likelihood is medium and impact is medium, and it is the risk most likely to appear in the same quarter as the margin number, which makes it hard to hedge with a position in the shares.

The seventh risk is governance and capital allocation. The company holds a large net-cash balance and pays out a fifth of profit; a controlling shareholder could redirect the cash through related-party purchases, raise the royalty, or leave the cash idle indefinitely [S2]. There is no evidence of abuse, because related-party flows are disclosed and proportionate, but the minority has no lever to force distribution [S2]. Likelihood is low and impact is medium, and it is why we value the operating business rather than the cash pile alone [S0].

Our bear case assumes down-trading persists, the rupiah stays weak and the gross margin stays near the third-quarter exit, so the group never earns a real operating margin, the fixed lease payment cannot be flexed and the dividend is cut. It carries the larger of the two tail weights and a value of Rp104 [S0]. Our base case holds the gross margin a point below the nine-month average rather than at the FY2024 like-for-like, grows revenue in line with a mature category and lifts capex to replacement; it carries the majority of the probability mass and a value of Rp734 [S0]. Our bull case assumes input costs roll over, the feminine and adult mix plus general trade lift revenue faster than the market, the margin returns toward the FY2024 like-for-like level and operating leverage brings SG&A down, with a value of Rp1,681 [S0]. Weighting the three in the ratio fifty-five, thirty, fifteen and applying the liquidity discount gives a target of Rp704, a 81.7% total return [S0]. The weights are the judgement call: the third quarter moved probability from the bull to the bear, and the base still holds the majority because the nine-month average and the FY2024 like-for-like both sit above our long-run margin.

The signposts that would change our view, in order: the fourth-quarter gross margin, which tells us whether the third-quarter break was a spike or a step; the FY2026 audited operating cash flow, which tells us whether the working-capital build reverses; any change in the parent royalty or related-party purchase terms; and the dividend declaration at the annual meeting, which tells us how the controlling shareholder intends to treat the cash [S2][S6]. A gross margin below our bear-case path for two consecutive quarters would move us to hold or sell regardless of the balance sheet, because the cash would then be the only thing left and the market already knows about it [S0].

Ownership is concentrated in three disclosed blocks: Unicharm Corporation holds 59.2%, PT APP Purinusa Ekapersada of the Sinar Mas group holds 20.8%, and the public holds 20.0% [S6]. The earlier reliance on a vendor insider figure was wrong and is corrected here: the annual report's share-ownership table and the share note are the authority, and the free float the market can actually trade is the 20.0% public block, not a residual [S6]. There is no dual-class structure and no intermediate holding company, but this is not a single-parent story: a second strategic holder with board seats and a supply relationship sits beside the Japanese parent. Its affiliate PT Pindo Deli Pulp and Paper Mills supplies materials to UCID, though the flow was 4.7 IDR bn in the first nine months, a small fraction of cost of revenue, and the APP bloc's nominees on the UCID board include executives of the wider Sinar Mas pulp and paper group [S2][S6]. Both the royalty relationship and the APP supply relationship are therefore minority risks, but the disclosed amounts put the APP tie well below the parent royalty in financial significance [S2]. The board is led by President Director Yasutaka Nishioka, and the annual report's governance section records the commissioners' review of the 2025 work plan and their conclusion that closer engagement was needed after the year's findings [S6]. That is a rare piece of candour from a controlled company and it is consistent with the operational problems described in the business section [S6].

Related-party dealings are the governance issue that matters here, and they are disclosed in detail. The company pays royalties to Unicharm Corporation and Unicharm Kokko Nonwoven under trademark and manufacturing licences, buys materials from group companies, and earns research-service income from the parent [S2]. The royalty was 168 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 and related-party purchases were 1.9% of cost of revenue, with related-party trade payables of a modest size on the balance sheet [S2]. We do not see evidence of value extraction beyond the disclosed terms, but the terms are set by the controlling shareholder and are therefore a permanent minority risk rather than a temporary one [S2]. No share pledge by the controlling shareholder is disclosed in the filings we hold [S6].

The audit is Big Four and the opinion history is clean. The FY2024 consolidated statements were audited by Siddharta Widjaja & Rekan, a member of the KPMG network, with an unqualified opinion dated 14 February 2025, and the FY2025 statements are included in the annual report with the independent auditor's report [S6]. The FY2025 auditor's report page is an image in the archived annual report and we could not extract the opinion text, so we rely on the FY2024 opinion and on the absence of any qualification, restatement or auditor change in the FY2025 disclosures [S6]. That is a limitation of our evidence and it is recorded here rather than glossed over.

The dividend record is short but consistent. The company pays a fifth of net profit, has paid a cash dividend every year since listing, paid 70.1 in FY2025 and 27.7 in 2026 despite the loss, and the payout policy is stated in the annual report and was followed through the loss year [S6][S2]. That is a positive governance signal: the controlling shareholder did not use the loss as a reason to stop paying the minority. The yield is low because the profit is low, and the policy means the dividend recovers with earnings rather than before them [S0].

ESG exposures are real but not material to the valuation. The company discloses quality, environmental and medical-device certifications, a solar-power installation at two factories that it says cuts thousands of tonnes of emissions a year, and product-level moves toward bio-material and organic-cotton feminine care [S6]. The main ESG risk is the single-use plastic profile of the product set, which regulators could tax or restrict, and the main opportunity is the adult-care and feminine-care mix, which aligns with an ageing population and with health awareness [S6]. We apply no ESG discount or premium; the disclosures are adequate and the exposures are ordinary for the category [S6].

The typical failure mode for a controlled consumer subsidiary in Indonesia is not fraud but indifference: the parent sets transfer prices and royalties to suit the group, the minority receives a policy dividend, and the shares trade at a persistent discount to book because there is no mechanism to close it. The counterweight is that the parent's own reputation and its long-run access to the Indonesian market depend on treating the listed vehicle fairly. An investor in this kind of name is underwriting the parent's incentives as much as the local franchise.

The nearest catalyst is the Q4 2026 trading update and the full-year result, expected in the first quarter of 2027. The number to watch is the fourth-quarter gross margin: two quarters above a fifth would confirm that the third-quarter break was a spike, while a second weak quarter would confirm the bear case [S2]. We also watch the operating cash flow line, because the nine-month figure of -9.2 IDR bn is the clearest evidence that the reported profit is not yet cash, and a reversal in the fourth quarter would restore confidence in earnings quality [S2].

The second catalyst is the FY2026 audited result and the proposed dividend, expected in March 2027 and put to the annual general meeting in April. The dividend matters less for its yield than for what it says about the controlling shareholder's intent: a payout at the stated fifth of profit on a recovered base would signal normalisation, while a cut would signal that the board expects margin pressure to persist [S6]. We also watch any disclosure on the parent royalty and related-party purchase terms, which are the largest controllable cost items outside the raw-material cycle [S2].

The third catalyst is the input-cost cycle. The house agri deck has the soft commodities it covers firm rather than falling into FY2027E, and polymer and pulp follow the same direction when the dollar is strong [S0][S8]. A turn in the rupiah or in pulp and polymer prices would be the fastest route to a margin beat, and the domestic superabsorbent-polymer capacity expansion scheduled for early 2027 is a specific event that could ease the input cost over the medium term [S8]. We would raise the gross-margin assumption on evidence of either, not in anticipation.

The KPIs we monitor between results, in order: the reported and like-for-like gross margin; the selling-expense ratio, which tells us whether the trade push is buying volume or just shelf space; the diaper and non-diaper segment split, because the mix shift is the profit story; operating cash flow and the working-capital build; capex as a share of revenue, because under-investment flatters free cash flow; and the cash balance, which is the floor under the valuation [S2][S6]. None of these needs a data subscription; they are all in the quarterly financial statements the company posts on its investor-relations site [S2].
